items.title: What an audit report is actually for
items.summary: A fund that collects thousands of crores and spends lakhs is not a scandal by arithmetic alone. It is a question about intent.

body.text: The number is not the story

Every few months a figure surfaces that looks damning on its own: money in, very little money out. The gap gets a headline, the headline gets a hashtag, and the argument ends there. But a balance is not a verdict. Funds are allowed to hold money. Endowments are supposed to. The question an audit exists to answer is narrower and harder: was the money held for a stated purpose, and does the holding match that purpose?
What to look for instead

Read the audit for three things. First, the mandate — what the fund said it would do with the money when it asked for it. Second, the disbursement schedule, which tells you whether slow spending was planned or simply happened. Third, the auditor's own language: statutory auditors are careful people, and a qualified opinion is a much louder signal than a large unspent balance.
Why this matters beyond one fund

Public money attracts two failures at once — the failure to spend it well, and the failure to scrutinise it well. A press cycle that treats every unspent rupee as theft trains readers to ignore the cases that are theft. Precision is not pedantry here. It is the only thing that makes the accusation mean anything when it is finally warranted.

items.title: After flood disasters, Nepal needs clear numbers on aid and a reconstruction plan
items.summary: Nepal’s flood-hit communities face a long road to recovery as damaged infrastructure, lost livelihoods, and questions over aid transparency complicate efforts to rebuild homes, restore services, and livelihoods.

body.text: Nepali communities live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities
Originally published on Global Voices
Settlements across the Tadi River, Devighat in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.

Forty-six days later, just when Nepal was trying to recover from the Bhotekoshi flash flood, which struck the Nepal–Tibet border regions, affecting Rasuwa and Nuwakot, another landslide-induced flood hit Chumnubri, Gorkha, on October 11, 2026. This latest disaster has added to the wounds of communities who live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities.

The climate-related disaster in Nuwakot has devastated a once-popular tourist landscape, destroying its natural beauty and economic opportunities, with settlements heartbreakingly reduced to rubble and vital infrastructure, including roads, bridges and hydro-power facilities, washed away. The full death toll remains officially unconfirmed.
Survivors still come to search for their belongings in Devighatm, Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.

But an uncomfortable truth lies behind the devastation: The human cost of such disasters often goes ignored. Behind the statistics are stories of broken dreams, lost livelihoods, buried memories. There are families trying to stay alive without their loved ones, communities faced with an uncertain future, and countless people trying to make lives reconnect and rebuild from what little is left.

The task of rebuilding is huge. The damage is not only to homes, roads and bridges, but also to farms and local businesses. Kyodo News reports via AP that 7,500 homes were damaged or completely destroyed, with costs of recovery hitting USD 4.77 billion. The government has now moved from emergency relief to rehabilitation and reconstruction and has also acknowledged the risks posed by possible glacial outburst floods (GLOFs) and other hazards. The destruction of bridges and transport links has made surviving communities vulnerable and slowed reconstruction, exposing residents to further risk.
Buildings left standing, and homes left empty in the Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.

To this end, joint efforts are underway to rebuild damaged infrastructure and restore vital services. But pledged assistance is not the same as money that has actually been received and delivered to affected communities. Nepal’s Ministry of Finance’s foreign assistance tracker shows that Nepal has received USD 24.89 million in disaster relief funds. Such tracking can help bring transparency to the collection and distribution of aid. The Prime Minister's Office separately reported that USD 50.47 million of assistance (cash, materials, and teams) had been pledged.

No formal update has been given on the implementation of longer-term reconstruction plans. Most of the aid is still going to meet immediate needs like medical aid, food, and temporary shelters, such as tents.
What are houses without their people called? Photo featuring reporter Susmita Aryal. Photo from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Maya Devi Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.

Many affected communities remain far from rebuilt infrastructure and restored livelihoods. India, China, the United States, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are providing assistance, and the Asian Development Bank and other international financial institutions have committed funds. Yet recovery is likely to progress unevenly. The challenge for affected communities is not just to rebuild what was lost but to restore livelihoods, public services and a sense of security in the face of recurring environmental hazards.

In the following photo essay, Global Voices highlights how Nepali citizens are still affected by the disaster. All photos were taken by Susmita Aryal in Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot District on October 7, 2026.
Tara Devi Tamang and others waiting for relief and basic needs provided at the Bidur Municipality Office, Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission
Daily essentials scattered around the community in Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission.
A half-destroyed shelter once used to be a home. Photo from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission.
Somebody’s whole world reduced to rubble. Image from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission.
A viral house broken window pane weaponized for an emergency flight. Image from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission.
Nothing is left of a riverside home in Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission.
A helmet sits alone without its rider. Image from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission.

items.title: Poetry book promotes Chabacano, Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language
items.summary: "The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.”

body.text: Ten authors and 23 poems are featured in the anthology
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo from the Facebook page of Voces del Alma. Used with permission

A new poetry anthology features writers of Chabacano, one of the Philippines’ 170 languages, which is widely spoken in the southernmost city of Zamboanga, and stands out as Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language.

The Philippines was a colony of Spain for more than three centuries, but the Spanish language was only used by the elite, friars, and colonial rulers. Only in Zamboanga did a Spanish-based creole language develop.

In 2018, Global Voices featured Bien Chabacano, a blog dedicated to promoting and documenting Chavacano de Zamboanga. Its creator, Jerome Herrera, launched a book project this year by inviting writers to submit poems to be compiled in an anthology. This led to the launch of the “Sombra y Luz” book in July, featuring 23 poems by 10 authors. The poems are mainly about love, family, and Zamboangueño identity.

Herrera said, “The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a literary language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.”

He added that the book title aims to convey a message of contrast about the changes in Zamboanga City. The book cover also provides a nostalgic reference to the flowers that decorated the city in the past.

The cover features an American-era style lamppost that can be seen along the Zamboanga boulevard. The cover also features bougainvilleas which my dad tells me were ubiquitous in Zamboanga City back when it was known as the Ciudad de Flores.
Herrera’s poem in the anthology mentions flowers and birds that enrich life in the city.
Maga pajaro que ta vola-vola, Na maga rama de pono ta queda, Alegre con uno y otro ta grita-grita, Twit! Twit! Twit! Entero el dia.
Mio pueblo Ciudad de Zamboanga, Ciudad de Flores que llama. De noche mucho pajaro ay columbra, Na maga cable de corriente ta esta.
Birds that fly and flutter freely, Perched upon the branches of trees, Singing and calling each other joyfully, Tweet! Tweet! Tweet! All day long.
Oh, my beloved City of Zamboanga, City of Flowers, they call you. At night, many birds can be found, Sitting on wires, that’s what they do.
In an interview with Global Voices, Herrera noted the heavy use of Spanish words in the selected poems:

…there is a lot of debate with regards to what Chabacano poetry should look like. For some, they like it with a lot of Spanish words and for others, they like it to be exactly as how Chabacano appears in everyday conversations. Most of the poems submitted leaned heavily on Spanish words, I think primarily because Chabacano writers rely on Spanish words to make their works sound more formal as well as more poetic. Since it’s poetry, I thought that it was alright to present Chabacano in an idealistic manner.
He added that the anthology seeks to encourage more people to accept the various ways that Chabacano is used.

For a very long time, people have been putting Chabacano inside a box. I hope that these books open up conversations regarding Chabacano literature and make people receptive to different kinds of writing styles in Chabacano.
This approach is evident in the poem “Escribi Chavacano, Conversa Chabacano,” which celebrates Chabacano as a living language.

Through references to poems, essays, fables, and the stories passed down by elders, the author reminds readers that the language continues to thrive when it is written, spoken, and shared with others.

The title itself is noteworthy for its use of both Chavacano and Chabacano, reflecting the coexistence of two accepted spellings of the language. In doing so, the poem highlights not only the importance of preserving Chabacano, but also the richness and diversity of its written tradition.
Herrera’s interview with Asymptote Journal noted the challenge of finding Chabacano contributors, and his hope that the book project can lead to more literary initiatives.

The biggest challenge is keeping the momentum going, since it’s hard to find Chavacano poets. Even so, I hope this anthology is just the beginning and that we’ll be able to publish a second volume in the future.

items.title: Archive: The Measurement of Time
items.summary: Misha Glenny chooses the first of his archive picks - bringing back classic conversations from the In Our Time archive, every Monday. Humans have tried to calculate, regulate, and measure time for thousands of years: from systems based on tracking sunrise and sunset, to the invention of increasingly precise mechanical alarm clocks and astrolabes. In this archive episode, first released in March 2012, Melvyn Bragg and guests discuss the methods used to measure time throughout human history. Early civilisations used the movements of heavenly bodies to tell the time, but in the ancient world there were also sophisticated timekeeping devices such as water clocks. The development of mechanical clocks in Europe emerged in the medieval period, when monks used such devices to sound an alarm to signal it was the hour to pray, although these clocks did not tell them the time. For hundreds of years clocks were inaccurate and it proved hard to remedy the problems, let alone settle on a standard time that a whole country should follow. It was the advent of the railways that meant time finally became standardised in Britain during the mid-19th century, and in 1884 Greenwich became the prime meridian of the world. items.title: Atlanta Dream and Hawks Announce Basketball Doubleheader at State Farm Arena
items.summary: The Atlanta Dream will host WNBA Finals Games 3 and 4 at State Farm Arena, alongside a basketball doubleheader with the Atlanta Hawks on October 24.

items.title: CIL Cup: Canning Dishahara F.A And Gobindadham Yoga & Sports Emerge As Howrah Zonal Champions
items.summary: Canning Dishahara F.A and Gobindadham Yoga & Sports have emerged as the men's and women's champions, respectively, at the Howrah zonal stage of the CIL Cup, an initiative of Coal India Limited. Both teams will represent their respective categories in the semifinals, which will be held in Purulia.

items.title: Ex-gang boss sentenced to 40 years for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder

also.title: Tupac Shakur killer sentenced to 40 years in prison
